# Preliminary Instructions

## How to Use This Primer

- Read Proverbs 1-9 four times.
- Read this primer, paying attention to is analysis of Proverbs 1-9.
- Thoughtfully consider, answer, and discuss the questions following each section.
- Record noteworthy ideas, questions, and observations.

## Executive Summary

Many read Proverbs for daily doses of wisdom; not many use it to build a foundation for spiritual formation. This primer on Proverbs 1-9 explores the beginning chapters of Proverbs as a biblical framework for spiritual formation in the wisdom tradition. It believes Proverbs is inspired divine revelation that is indispensably useful for personal Christian growth and shepherding duties of those who oversee the spiritual formation of others. Inasmuch as Proverbs offers the content of wisdom, Proverbs 1-9 establishes a foundation on the mean of how one grows in wisdom. Essentially, the first nine chapters of Proverbs offers a theology of formation. The theological underpinnings of this section incubate practical principles of faith and moral development. Once the structure, substance, and intent of Proverbs 1-9 is rightly understood, parents, teachers, pastors, and mentors will find the Solomon's ancient compendium timeless and relevant, offering superlative insight into faith formation, spiritual pilgrimage, rites of passage, spiritual pedagogy, and portraits of biblical masculinity and femininity.

## Introduction

The Christian life is not for the faint of heart. To live in a fallen world requires nerve and conviction. To renounce idols and refrain from immorality demands courage to pursue a countercultural mode of living and fearlessness to embrace an exilic identity. To raise our mast under the banner of Christ and his church calls for selfless sacrifice and a bold servant spirit. We prioritize self-rule so that we can make ourselves a slave to Christ—and a servant to all. To raise children in the fear of the Lord and cultivate homes adorned with biblical values calls for patient endurance and undying loyalty to our heavenly Father, the risen Christ, and the indwelling Holy Spirit. To live a life of faith is to overcome hardship, endure suffering, and be faithful until the end. Christians do not mature in spite of struggle; they grow in the midst of adversity.

The road to faith maturity is a path of immense difficulty—duty tested in tribulation, character refined by affliction, faith proven under trial, purity gained by overcoming temptation, and hope exercised as a defiant insistence that Christ will win in the end. The mature Christian life is marked by these manifold qualities and priceless virtues. But this bold vision for a fortified faith cannot be realized without a key biblical virtue—a biblical virtue amply and urgently commended by Scripture. The mature Christian embodies a life of wisdom. Although not commonly associated together, wisdom and faith formation are inextricably bound together. All manner of boldness, bravery, and spiritual brawn will be of no use if it is not ruled by a life of wisdom. The world is a dangerous place, fraught with lurking enemies and rival kingdoms. Only the wise can navigate the perilous terrain of this world as a faithful citizen of God's kingdom.

In the Bible, Proverbs is a boundless treasury of wisdom. Many laud Proverbs for its accessible kernels of inspired wisdom. Situational proverbs that unlock "how life works best" are usually one of the common "first contact points" with Proverbs. But when it comes to letting Proverbs set an agenda for faith formation and moral development, it is drastically underutilized. Many wrongly relegate the mere idea of wisdom and philosophy to the realm of lofty abstraction—questions of intrigue for imposing intellects but not germane to those who live in the real world. Moreover, many are unable to see how wisdom and discipleship connect. While many view discipleship as a grounding in the essentials of the faith, they view wisdom as some second-order spiritual attainment. In addition to these common misconceptions, popular Christianity has adopted a generic, androgynous spirituality—depictions of faith maturity that unhelpfully make no distinction between godly men and women.

In what follows, we will explore the unique canonical and theological purpose of Proverbs. By exploring Proverbs 1-9—rightly understanding it to be a introduction to faith formation—we will see the indispensable usefulness of this portion of Scripture. Essentially, this primer attempts to commend Proverbs as vital for building a framework for faith and moral development. This task is of paramount importance. To become wise and mature in the faith we need to understand the content and the means of faith formation. Without this foundation, churches, parents, pastors, and disciples will remain ceaselessly juvenile. We need to both understand what wisdom is as well as how to grow in wisdom. Proverbs offers both. Therefore, in the following primer, we target several aims: 1. establish the literary and occasional context of Proverbs, 2. explore Proverbs as a coherent vision for faith formation in the wisdom tradition, 3. unearth the root metaphor of journey and quest, 4. consider the unique importance of rites of passage for formation, 5. commend Proverbs 1-9 as a blueprint for developing a holistic spiritual pedagogy, and 6. explore the unique portraits of masculinity and femininity offered to us.
